result: In slowly growing E. coli, ori is maintained at mid-cell from birth until replication, after which duplicated origins experience cohesion for 10-15 minutes and then migrate to opposite quarter positions.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C9-C11) describe established knowledge about ori positioning in E. coli that is well-supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work. This provides the biological context for the study.

result: MukBEF, a functional homolog of SMC complexes, forms dynamic clusters at mid-cell or quarter positions that are closely associated with ori, recruit Topo IV, and are required for proper ori positioning.
evaluation: These claims (C12-C25) summarize established knowledge about MukBEF from prior work, supported by extensive citations. This provides the mechanistic foundation for the authors' model and is well-established in the literature.

result: A stochastic Turing pattern with flux-balance mechanism can explain MukBEF cluster positioning, with short cells having a single center-positioned peak and longer cells having quarter-positioned peaks.
evaluation: These claims (C26-C30) reference the authors' previous work (Murray and Sourjik, 2017) which established the Turing mechanism for MukBEF positioning. This is appropriately cited and provides the theoretical framework for the current study.

result: MukBEF foci and ori are more colocalized than expected if positioned independently (r=0.8), and ori experiences greater restoring velocity toward MukBEF foci than toward mid-cell, indicating that MukBEF positions ori.
evaluation: These claims (C34-C38) are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-d, including statistical analysis comparing measured versus expected distributions and velocity profile analysis. The conclusion that MukBEF positions ori is well-supported by both current and cited experimental evidence.

result: MukBEF foci display similar biases toward ori and mid-cell, suggesting bi-directional attraction between MukBEF and ori.
evaluation: These claims (C39-C40) are supported by velocity profile analysis shown in Figure 1e. The inference of bi-directional attraction is reasonable given the data, though the authors appropriately use cautious language ('may be').

result: The authors propose that MukBEF is preferentially loaded onto the chromosome within the ori region, analogous to SMC loading at parS sites in B. subtilis, though no ParB/parS analogue has been discovered in E. coli.
evaluation: Claim C42 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis ('we propose') that will be tested computationally. While C43 provides precedent from other bacteria, C44 acknowledges the lack of direct evidence in E. coli. This is a key assumption of the model that requires experimental validation.

result: Stochastic simulations show that ori tracks the self-organized MukBEF focus to mid-cell, reproducing linear velocity profiles and achieving good agreement with experimental diffusion constants and drift rates by adjusting only two parameters.
evaluation: These claims (C45-C48) are supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The model successfully reproduces key experimental observations with minimal parameter fitting, and the calculated restoring force (0.02 pN) is comparable to other partitioning systems.

result: Preferential loading of MukBEF at ori (at intermediate levels around 6x) suppresses noise in positioning, increases colocalization with ori, and shows excellent agreement with experimental ori position distributions and velocity profiles.
evaluation: These claims (C49-C53) are supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2e-f and Figure 2—figure supplements 4-5. The identification of 6x preferential loading as optimal is based on multiple metrics including variance, colocalization, and agreement with experimental data.

result: Without preferential loading, approximately half of simulations have both oris at the same quarter position, but preferential loading (>6x) results in stable and accurate partitioning by changing the stability of different steady states.
evaluation: These claims (C54-C58) are supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3a-c. The model demonstrates that preferential loading is necessary for accurate partitioning, with quantitative analysis of partitioning accuracy and stability as a function of loading ratio.

result: In growing cells, combining preferential loading with short-range entropic repulsion between newly replicated oris is necessary and sufficient to reproduce observed partitioning dynamics, with good agreement in segregation velocity and partitioning accuracy time-courses.
evaluation: These claims (C59-C69) are supported by extensive parameter sweeps (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and comparison with experimental data (Figure 4e-f). The model demonstrates that both mechanisms are required: entropic repulsion alone (C65) or preferential loading alone (C59-C60) are insufficient, but together they reproduce experimental observations.

result: Polymer simulations demonstrate that spatially-varying looping probability (representing MukBEF-mediated DNA bridging) can generate directed movement of ori toward MukBEF foci through elastic fluctuations, accelerate ori segregation, and position oris to opposite quarter positions.
evaluation: These claims (C70-C80) are supported by polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5. The simulations provide a plausible physical mechanism for the biased diffusion assumed in the stochastic model, showing that looping probability gradients can generate directed motion and proper positioning.

result: The self-organizing MukBEF gradient with preferential loading at ori can accurately reproduce observed ori dynamics without any actual directed force, with accurate partitioning emerging as a property of the system through mutual attraction between MukBEF foci and ori.
evaluation: These claims (C81-C85) summarize the main findings and are well-supported by the combined stochastic and polymer simulation results. The emphasis on self-organization without directed forces (C83) is a key conceptual contribution, though the mechanism underlying the mutual attraction remains to be fully elucidated experimentally.

result: Ori specificity must be encoded by sequences within the ori region (not oriC itself), and the authors predict that inserting this centromeric sequence into a plasmid would cause colocalization with MukBEF foci.
evaluation: Claim C86 is a logical inference, C87 is supported by citation, but C88 is an untested prediction. This represents a testable hypothesis that could validate or refute the model's assumptions about preferential loading.

result: The model can recapitulate ori positioning during faster growth with multiple replication forks when accounting for higher MukBEF copy numbers, with ori and MukBEF remaining tightly associated.
evaluation: These claims (C89, C91) are supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The model's ability to extend to multi-fork replication strengthens its generality, though experimental validation of these predictions would be valuable.

result: Both ori and MukB foci are confined to the center 40% of the cell width (approximately 300 nm), and MukBEF has an arc length of about 70 nm, justifying the one-dimensional modeling approach.
evaluation: These claims (C92-C95) are supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-g and citation to structural work. This provides justification for the one-dimensional simulation approach, though the authors acknowledge limitations of this simplification.

result: Cells were treated with DL serine hydroxamate (SHX) to inhibit replication initiation and enrich for cells with a single ori focus, resulting in cells with mean length 2.2 μm.
evaluation: These claims (C96-C98) describe the experimental methodology and are supported by the methods section and Figure 1 caption. The use of SHX is appropriate for enriching single-ori cells and is supported by citation.

result: MukBEF requires ATP to establish a self-organized gradient but is not pulled by active forces; ori attraction up the gradient may arise from energetic considerations and chromosome elasticity resulting in effective directed motion.
evaluation: These claims (C31-C33) describe key conceptual features of the model. C31 is consistent with known MukBEF biochemistry, C32 is a defining feature of self-organization, and C33 is a mechanistic hypothesis tested by the polymer simulations (claims C70-C80).

result: Co-localization with MukBEF is strongest for ori and becomes progressively weaker for ori-distant loci.
evaluation: This claim (C41) is supported by citation to previous experimental work (Danilova et al., 2007) and provides additional evidence for the special relationship between MukBEF and ori.

result: A non-trivial feedback between self-organizing MukBEF gradients and oris leads to accurate ori positioning, with the model finding excellent agreement with experiments and confirming that oris exhibit biased motion toward MukBEF clusters.
evaluation: These claims (C5-C8) represent the main conclusions of the paper and are well-supported by the combined experimental and computational results. The agreement between model and experiment is demonstrated across multiple metrics (position distributions, velocity profiles, partitioning accuracy).
